chunks: How a GPU works. The question: How does a GPU work?
You write a small program called a kernel for one thread, then launch it across thousands or millions of threads. The hardware bundles threads into groups of 32 called warps.
A warp runs one instruction on all 32 of its lanes (small arithmetic units) at once.
When a warp must wait for memory, the GPU switches to another ready warp, so the waiting is hidden by having many threads.
Picture one chef tending many pots. While one pot simmers, which is like waiting for memory, the chef stirs another, so no time is wasted.
The more pots there are, the less the chef ever stands idle. One difference: the 32 lanes in a warp must all do the same step together, like 32 burners controlled by one knob.
The block scheduler decouples the program from the machine size. Blocks are independent, so any number of SMs can work on them.
Within an SM, the warp scheduler (not the program) chooses which warp issues each cycle.
Kernel: the function launched on the GPU and run by many threads. Warp: a group of 32 threads that execute the same instruction together.
Latency hiding: switching to another warp while one waits, so the processor stays busy. Divergence: lanes in one warp wanting different branches. The warp runs each path in turn.
Coalescing: merging neighboring threads' memory reads into one wide read.
Say a memory load takes 400 cycles, and a warp does about 10 independent instructions between loads.
To keep the processor busy, it needs roughly 400 / 10 = 40 other warps ready to run. That is why a GPU keeps thousands of threads resident. Memory pattern matters too.
If 32 threads read 32 consecutive 4-byte numbers, that is 128 bytes in one transaction. If they read scattered addresses, it takes up to 32 transactions, and bandwidth collapses.
That is the whole idea: hide waiting with parallelism, and keep threads in step.
"You write a kernel for one thread and launch it over a huge grid. The hardware groups threads into warps of 32 that run the same instruction in lockstep on an SM.
Each SM holds many warps, and when one stalls on memory the scheduler instantly issues another, so latency is hidden by parallelism.
Divergent branches and uncoalesced memory accesses are what cost performance."
